articles.title: Three Firms Walked Into A Merger And The World’s Biggest Law Firm Walked Out
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

Dentons is the largest law firm in the world by headcount, but it didn’t exist as such until 2013, when three separate firms, from three different countries, combined all at once to create it (its later mergers, including the 2015 Dacheng tie-up, only built on that foundation). Name the three firms that merged in 2013 to form the Biglaw firm known as Dentons.

Hint: The trio spanned the Atlantic and then some: a transatlantic U.S./U.K. firm whose name survives in “Dentons,” a French firm, and a Canadian one. The U.S./U.K. piece was itself the product of a 2010 merger.

See the answer on the next page.

The post Three Firms Walked Into A Merger And The World’s Biggest Law Firm Walked Out appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Legal Ethics Roundup: Solo Lawyer Well-Being Paradox, Habba Ethics Complaint, Judge Removed, Plagiarism In Judicial Application, Billable Hour Shake-Up, AI Sanctions & More
articles.content:
Ed. note: Please welcome Renee Knake Jefferson back to the pages of Above the Law. Subscribe to her Substack, Legal Ethics Roundup, here.
I’m writing this week’s LER from sunny Palm Springs, after wrapping up a meeting of the ABA Accreditation Council. As reported by Reuters, the Council “adopted a slate of proposals that eliminate or roll back key accreditation rules for law schools — part of its wider effort to bolster innovation and reduce what it has called ‘undue burdens’ on schools.” Read the full article here.
I was fortunate to avoid Friday’s ground stop during my travels, but I saw posts from several LER readers stranded at airports across the country. I hope everyone has since made it safely to their destinations, and that the week ahead involves considerably less time in airport terminals!
#1 “Solo Lawyers Have a Well-Being Blueprint the Profession Needs.” From Denise Robinson in Bloomberg Law: “Over the last decade, the legal profession has dedicated much-needed attention to mental health. But the conversation has mostly tilted toward Big Law. The vast majority of lawyers in private practice don’t work for large law firms. They’re solo practitioners or work in small or mid-size firms with a different mix of benefits and challenges affecting their well-being. Solo practitioners scored highest of any legal work environment on measures of depression, anxiety, and stress, with most experiencing high occupational burnout, according to a 2026 report from the American Bar Association. However, the 2025 ALPS Solo Well-Being Report also found solo practitioners reported high levels of happiness and satisfaction, largely driven by autonomy and control over their practices. The numbers may seem contradictory, but they aren’t. Attorney well-being and satisfaction aren’t the absence of distress.” Read more here.
#2 “Board: U.S. Attorney Plagiarized Application to Become a Judge.” From the Iowa Capital Dispatch: “Federal prosecutor is reprimanded for ‘extensive’ copying of application. A federal prosecutor based in Cedar Rapids has been sanctioned for allegedly plagiarizing portions of his application to become a district court judge. The Attorney Disciplinary Board of the Supreme Court of Iowa alleges that in May 2026, Michael S.A. Hudson, who works as a special assistant United States attorney for the U.S. Attorney’s Office in the Northern District of Iowa, applied for an open position as a district court judge within Iowa’s First Judicial District. According to the board, ‘significant portions of the application were copied from application materials Judge Justin Lightfoot had submitted when seeking a judicial appointment in 2021.’” Read more here.
#3 “Trump Ally Alina Habba Mildon Faces New Jersey Attorney Ethics Complaint.” From Reuters: “A former lawyer for President Donald Trump is facing a professional disciplinary complaint in New Jersey over allegations that she improperly inserted herself in a workplace sexual harassment dispute at one of his private golf clubs where she was a paying member.” Read more here.
#4 “Judicial Watch Founder Klayman Disbarred at Supreme Court.” From Bloomberg Law: “The US Supreme Court barred Judicial Watch founder Larry Klayman from practicing law at the high court. The justices on Monday disbarred Klayman at the court in an unsigned disciplinary order. He was previously suspended from practicing before the justices in June following suspensions in Washington and Florida in recent years over alleged ethical breaches. Klayman has said those decisions were flawed. Klayman told Bloomberg Law that the Supreme Court’s order isn’t final and he plans to file a motion for reconsideration.” Read more here.
#5 “Baker McKenzie Looks to Abandon the Billable Hour as Default.” From The Wall Street Journal: “Law firm Baker McKenzie is shifting away from billing clients by the hour as a default, a sign of how artificial intelligence is upending traditional payment structures in the legal industry. The firm has begun charging clients on a value-based billing model, according to Global Chair Sunny Mann. When pivoting toward solutions aided by technology and the use of AI, charging by the hour doesn’t always make sense anymore, he said.” Read more here (gift link).
#6 “LA County Judge Robert Draper Removed for Willful Misconduct.” From Courthouse News Service: “The California Commission on Judicial Performance cited, among other instances of misconduct, the judge’s rambling discourse on race relations and Black football players when a Black attorney made her first appearance before him.” Read more here.
#7 “‘My Client Is Often the Truth’: Neil Barofsky on What Matters Most.” From The American Lawyer: “For Neil Barofsky, co-head of the monitorship practice at Jenner & Block and a finalist for The American Lawyer’s Attorney of the Year, independence means committing to the truth, above everything else, without being tempted or turned toward an easier path.” Read more here.
#8 “2 Attys Fined For AI Citation Errors But Local Counsel Spared.” From Law360: “A Delaware federal magistrate judge said that three attorneys violated rules of professional conduct after the court discovers legal authorities that were falsely generated by artificial intelligence in a brief last year, issuing $3,000 sanctions against just two of them after local counsel said he received the filing at the last minute but took responsibility for its errors anyway.” Read more here.
#9 “KY Federal Judge Nominee Accused of Misconduct During Time in State Court.” From the Louisville Courier Journal: “The Kentucky circuit court judge nominated by President Donald Trump for a federal role is facing allegations of misconduct, according to a filing by the state’s Judicial Conduct Commission, over claims he violated the duties of his office.” Read more here.
#10 “Raskin Seeks Judiciary Gavel, High Court Ethics Curbs.” From Law360: “In making his bid to be elected House Judiciary chair, Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., on Friday said ethics reforms for the U.S. Supreme Court are among his top priorities.” Read more here.
Some of the most pressing questions in my professional life right now concern the future of higher education and the responsibilities of those entrusted with leading it. This week, I’ll be in Nashville for “Trusteeship and the Future of the American University,” a gathering hosted at Vanderbilt University exploring academic freedom, free speech, institutional neutrality, scholarly standards, accreditation, public trust, and the fiduciary duties of trustees. These issues sit at the intersection of my work as a legal ethics scholar, a university trustee, and a member of the national accreditor of law schools. I’m especially interested in how governing boards can navigate political pressures while protecting academic freedom, institutional independence, and the integrity of higher education.
Looking for other upcoming ethics events? You’ll find a list here.
Renee Knake Jefferson holds the endowed Doherty Chair in Legal Ethics and is a Professor of Law at the University of Houston. Check out more of her writing at the Legal Ethics Roundup. Find her on X (formerly Twitter) at @reneeknake or Bluesky at legalethics.bsky.social.
The post Legal Ethics Roundup: Solo Lawyer Well-Being Paradox, Habba Ethics Complaint, Judge Removed, Plagiarism In Judicial Application, Billable Hour Shake-Up, AI Sanctions & More appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Why Everything Looks Chaotic From The GC’s Desk
articles.content:
Imagine opening your inbox to a customer escalation, a product question, a contract exception, and a request for board materials. Each has a different owner. Each has a different deadline. All four need an answer today.
Now suppose they involve the same thing: the company has started describing an AI feature in a way its product documentation does not support.
Sales encounters the problem as a customer expectation. Product encounters it as an ambiguous requirement. Legal encounters it as contract language. The board encounters it as a question about oversight.
Four requests. One possible connection worth investigating.
That is the image behind a series I am calling “Above the Crossing.” Picture a GC standing amid the multidirectional movement of Shibuya Crossing in Tokyo. At street level, the most urgent task is avoiding the next collision. From a higher vantage point, routes and recurring points of convergence become easier to notice.
I use the image because a legal inbox organizes work by arrival. It offers very little help understanding how the work was produced.
A request that arrives on Thursday may have begun with a product decision made in February. Another request, arriving minutes later, may reflect a commercial commitment made yesterday. Their simultaneous arrival tells you almost nothing about their relationship.
Even the labels can get in the way. “Commercial,” “privacy,” and “product” are useful for assigning lawyers. They can separate matters that depend on the same fact, owner, or unresolved decision.
Eric Dodson Greenberg’s writing about the GC’s enterprise perspective provides a useful starting point for looking across those boundaries. My work on trust architecture asks what organizations can build once related governance problems become visible.
Here is where I would start: keep a small second record alongside the matter queue.
The queue asks who needs an answer and when. The second record asks what had to be true for the request to become necessary. Was a business rule missing? Was the technical answer unavailable? Did someone have responsibility without authority? Had an earlier decision quietly expired?
Use the requester’s language before assigning a category. “We need approval again because nobody knows whether the exception applies to this customer” is more informative than “contract review.”
Then look for repeats across a defined set of matters. A handful of examples can suggest a hypothesis. It takes further checking to establish whether the apparent connection is real.
In the hypothetical AI-feature problem, talk to the people who maintain the feature, the sales materials, and the customer commitments. Perhaps there is no approved description. Perhaps one exists and is difficult to find. Perhaps the description is accurate, and the customer is asking for something genuinely new.
Each possibility calls for a different response. Sending another warning about careful wording will do little for an inaccessible source. Creating another source can make version confusion worse.
There is also a visibility problem to keep in mind. The legal inbox contains the matters people chose to send to legal. Review some comparable decisions that proceeded elsewhere. They may show a workable approach, an unreported problem, or a reason your initial explanation is incomplete.
The immediate requests still need attention. Getting above the crossing does not excuse leaving people stranded inside it. The discipline is to preserve enough context while resolving the matter that the organization can learn something from its recurrence.
By the end of the week, the useful question is: which repeated request now has an explanation we can test?
Choose one. Find the person who owns the relevant condition. Change that condition on a limited basis and watch what happens.
The inbox will continue to fill. Over time, some of its contents should become more intelligible. That is the beginning of an architectural view of legal work.
Olga V. Mack is the CEO of TermScout, an AI-powered contract certification platform that accelerates revenue and eliminates friction by certifying contracts as fair, balanced, and market-ready. A serial CEO and legal tech executive, she previously led a company through a successful acquisition by LexisNexis. Olga is also a Fellow at CodeX, The Stanford Center for Legal Informatics, and the Generative AI Editor at law.MIT. She is a visionary executive reshaping how we law—how legal systems are built, experienced, and trusted. Olga teaches at Berkeley Law, lectures widely, and advises companies of all sizes, as well as boards and institutions. An award-winning general counsel turned builder, she also leads early-stage ventures including Virtual Gabby (Better Parenting Plan), Product Law Hub, ESI Flow, and Notes to My (Legal) Self, each rethinking the practice and business of law through technology, data, and human-centered design. She has authored The Rise of Product Lawyers, Legal Operations in the Age of AI and Data, Blockchain Value, and Get on Board, with Visual IQ for Lawyers (ABA) forthcoming. Olga is a 6x TEDx speaker and has been recognized as a Silicon Valley Woman of Influence and an ABA Woman in Legal Tech. Her work reimagines people’s relationship with law—making it more accessible, inclusive, data-driven, and aligned with how the world actually works. She is also the host of the Notes to My (Legal) Self podcast (streaming on Spotify, Apple Podcasts, and YouTube), and her insights regularly appear in Forbes, Bloomberg Law, Newsweek, VentureBeat, ACC Docket, and Above the Law. She earned her B.A. and J.D. from UC Berkeley. Follow her on LinkedIn and X @olgavmack.

articles.title: Realize Your Mistake Late — But Don’t Expect Us To Be Impressed
articles.content:
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is a hoot.
She was the wokest of the woke a half-dozen years ago, leading the charge for Woke 1: Defund the police. Don’t prosecute shoplifters. Avoid microaggressions. Defend the term “woke” itself against attacks.
But now she’s realized that Woke 1 went too far: “Woke 1 was crazy.“
You don’t say.
Congratulations, AOC! You’ve caught on. But I’d rather support someone who was intelligent enough to see the truth all along.
I’m not ideological about this; it cuts in all directions.
Although Megyn Kelly was hardly the worst, she was only too willing to spread misleading electoral narratives in 2020 and 2021. But now, when Donald Trump tries to pull the same stunt and insist that the 2026 elections were stolen, she tells him to “Just stop.“
Do tell.
Congratulations, Megyn! You’ve caught on. But I’d rather hear opinion commentary from someone who was intelligent enough to see the truth all along.
Michael Cohen thought that Trump was the cat’s meow. And then he thought that Trump was a criminal who threatened democracy. And now he again thinks that Trump was OK. And in five years, when Trump’s inexplicable luster has vanished, Cohen will change his mind yet again.
Do people really listen to clowns like this?
I promise you that, within five or 10 years, you’ll be hearing from Republicans telling you that they’ve realized that Trump was a clownish buffoon all along.
Is that a fact?
Congratulations, Republicans! You’ll have seen the light.
But why didn’t you realize that Trump was a clownish buffoon from the very start? Wasn’t it obvious to anyone willing to pay attention — like JD Vance, for example — that Trump might have been “America’s Hitler“? (I think Vance has since changed his mind about that. But maybe not. And who knows what Vance will realize when he’s trying to win the 2028 or 2032 Republican primaries?)
Vance wasn’t alone. Weren’t a few never-Trump Republicans telling you in 2016 that Trump was an idiot? And wasn’t just about every Democrat saying that? But it took until now for you to catch on?
To the future Republican turncoats: You might see the truth about Trump five years from now, but I won’t be impressed.
I also won’t be impressed about all the policy issues on which you flipped your opinion to support Trump and will flip your opinion again in the future: Across-the-board tariffs were a bad idea. The federal debt is a problem. Appeasing Russia is a fool’s game. Canada’s on our side. The war in Iran wasn’t such a good idea, after all.
I don’t like folks who sense the blowing political (or intellectual) winds and then decide that their opinions were wrong in the past. I prefer folks intelligent enough to understand the truth as we’re living things.
Mark Herrmann spent 17 years as a partner at a leading international law firm and later oversaw litigation, compliance and employment matters at a large international company. He is the author of The Curmudgeon’s Guide to Practicing Law and Drug and Device Product Liability Litigation Strategy (affiliate links). You can reach him by email at inhouse@abovethelaw.com.

Vance wasn’t alone. Weren’t a few never-Trump Republicans telling you in 2016 that Trump was an idiot? And wasn’t just about every Democrat saying that? But it took until now for you to catch on?

To the future Republican turncoats: You might see the truth about Trump five years from now, but I won’t be impressed.

I also won’t be impressed about all the policy issues on which you flipped your opinion to support Trump and will flip your opinion again in the future: Across-the-board tariffs were a bad idea. The federal debt is a problem. Appeasing Russia is a fool’s game. Canada’s on our side. The war in Iran wasn’t such a good idea, after all.

I don’t like folks who sense the blowing political (or intellectual) winds and then decide that their opinions were wrong in the past. I prefer folks intelligent enough to understand the truth as we’re living things.
